(CNN) -- At 44-years-old Abhisit Vejjajiva is Thailand's youngest prime minister in more than 60 years. But perhaps more immediately significantly, he is the country's third prime minister in four months after a period of immense upheaval in Thailand. After just two days of taking office, Thai PM Abhisit Vejjajiva talked to CNN's Dan Rivers for Talk Asia. Thailand's recent political turmoil, which included national demonstrations and the forced closures of international airports, dates back to the 2006 coup that overthrew former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, the former People's Power Party leader. In September, the Constitutional Court forced out his replacement Samak Sundaravej, finding that he had violated the constitution by appearing as a paid guest on a television cooking show. In turn he was replaced by Thaksin's brother-in-law, Somchai Wongsawat, who immediately found himself beset by opposition demonstrations that accused him of leading a proxy government for Thaksin. He too was thrown out by a Constitutional Court ruling. Abhisit was named as the new Prime Minister on December 15, and his biggest challenge will be to steady a country that until recently was known as one of the most region's most stable. A career politician, Abhisit was born in Newcastle in the north east of England to wealthy Thai-Chinese parents and attended Eton, one of the UK's top private schools before studying politics, philosophy and economics at Oxford University. While highly critical of the corruption and cronyism in Thai politics, Abhisit's own route to power has not been as he may have wanted it. As leader of the Democrat Party since 2005, he failed to win either of the elections he contended. He was chosen by the Thai parliament to be Prime Minister during a special session. His selection was contingent on support of factions from the now banned PPP who changed allegiance, many of whom he had previously criticized. Abhisit now leads a coalition government with a small majority consisting of a number of parties and interests, leading political commentators to speculate about the length of his tenure in office, many suggesting more than a year in power would be a success. Countering accusations of inexperience, Abhisit can still boast 17 years of political practice, having become a parliamentarian at the age of 27. As well as being young and cosmopolitan, he has gained a reputation as being above the sleaze and corruption that has dogged many other Thai politicians, while he publicly opposed the bloodless military coup that removed Thaksin from office 2006. However critics have said that his policies are borrowed heavily from Thaksin and that his party's decision to boycott the snap election in 2006 led to the constitutional crisis and coup against Thaksin. Most of Abhisit's support comes from the educated middle classes and gaining support, or at least lessening the divisions between sections of Thai society is something he has been immediately faced with. "He needs to send a clear signal of change that he is a leader who will reach out to all," said Bunranaj Smutharak, a spokesman for Abhisit's Democrat Party. "We are confident the long turmoil over the past two years will be brought to an end by this change in government," he said. "What we set out to do is reunite the country."

(CNN) — At age 44, Abhisit Vejjajiva has become Thailand’s youngest prime minister in over six decades. Even more pressing, however, is that he is the nation’s third leader in just four months, following a time of severe political instability. Only two days after assuming the post, Abhisit spoke with CNN’s Dan Rivers on *Talk Asia*.

The unrest that has recently shaken Thailand — including mass protests and the shutdown of international airports — can be traced to the 2006 military coup that removed former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, who had led the People’s Power Party. In September, the Constitutional Court dismissed Thaksin’s successor, Samak Sundaravej, ruling that he had breached the constitution by accepting payment to appear on a televised cooking program.

Samak was then succeeded by Somchai Wongsawat, Thaksin’s brother-in-law. Somchai quickly became the target of opposition protests, with demonstrators claiming he was heading a government that merely acted on Thaksin’s behalf. He, too, was removed from office by a Constitutional Court decision.

Abhisit was appointed prime minister on December 15. His foremost task will be to restore stability to a country that, until recently, had been regarded as one of the region’s most politically steady nations.

A lifelong politician, Abhisit was born in Newcastle, in northeast England, to affluent Thai-Chinese parents. He was educated at Eton, one of Britain’s most prestigious private schools, and later studied politics, philosophy and economics at Oxford University.

Although Abhisit has often condemned corruption and patronage in Thai politics, the way he reached the premiership was not necessarily the path he might have preferred. He has led the Democrat Party since 2005, but did not win either of the elections in which he competed. Instead, he was selected as prime minister by Thailand’s parliament during a special session.

His rise depended on backing from factions of the now-dissolved PPP that switched sides — including many figures he had criticized in the past. Abhisit now heads a coalition government with only a narrow majority, made up of several parties and interest groups. That has led political analysts to question how long he can remain in power, with many suggesting that lasting more than a year would itself count as a success.

In response to claims that he lacks experience, Abhisit can point to 17 years in politics, having first entered parliament at 27. In addition to his youth and international background, he has developed an image as a politician largely untouched by the sleaze and corruption that have affected many of his Thai counterparts. He also publicly opposed the bloodless 2006 military coup that ousted Thaksin.

Still, detractors argue that many of his policies closely resemble Thaksin’s. They also say the Democrat Party’s choice to boycott the 2006 snap election helped create the constitutional crisis that ultimately led to the coup against Thaksin.

Abhisit’s base of support lies largely among educated middle-class voters. One of the first challenges before him is to broaden that backing — or at least reduce the deep divisions within Thai society.

“He needs to send a clear signal of change that he is a leader who will reach out to all,” said Bunranaj Smutharak, a spokesman for Abhisit’s Democrat Party.

“We are confident the long turmoil over the past two years will be brought to an end by this change in government,” he added. “What we set out to do is reunite the country.”

counterfactuals.output:
**Abhisit Vejjajiva takes power in Thailand after months of political turmoil**

*Bangkok, Thailand* — Abhisit Vejjajiva, the Oxford-educated leader of Thailand’s Democrat Party, has become prime minister at a moment of deep political division, economic uncertainty and public fatigue after months of unrest that paralyzed parts of the country and exposed a bitter struggle over Thailand’s democratic future.

Abhisit’s rise came after a parliamentary vote in December 2008, following a court ruling that dissolved the ruling People Power Party and forced then-Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat from office. The decision reshaped the political landscape and allowed the Democrats to assemble a coalition government with defecting factions and smaller parties.

His appointment ends one phase of Thailand’s crisis — but it does not resolve the larger conflict between supporters and opponents of former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, whose influence has dominated Thai politics since his ouster in a 2006 military coup.

## A country shaken by protests

Thailand’s latest political upheaval reached a dramatic peak when anti-government protesters from the People’s Alliance for Democracy, or PAD, occupied Bangkok’s two main airports in late 2008. The shutdown stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers, damaged the country’s tourism industry and delivered a major blow to Thailand’s international image.

The PAD, often known as the “Yellow Shirts,” accused the government of being a proxy for Thaksin, who remained popular among rural and working-class voters but was reviled by many in Bangkok’s middle class, conservative elites and parts of the establishment.

The airport occupations followed months of street protests, clashes and political deadlock. Earlier in the year, another Thaksin-aligned prime minister, Samak Sundaravej, was removed by a court after being found to have violated rules by hosting television cooking shows while in office.

For many Thais, the turmoil underscored a recurring pattern: elected governments linked to Thaksin winning at the ballot box, only to face street protests, court rulings or military pressure that undermined their ability to govern.

## Who is Abhisit Vejjajiva?

Abhisit, born in Newcastle, England, in 1964 to a family of Thai medical professionals, has long been seen as one of Thailand’s most polished political figures. Educated at Eton College and Oxford University, where he studied philosophy, politics and economics, he returned to Thailand and entered politics at a young age.

He became a member of parliament in the early 1990s and rose through the ranks of the Democrat Party, Thailand’s oldest political party. Known for his articulate English, calm demeanor and technocratic image, Abhisit built a reputation as a reform-minded conservative.

But he has also faced criticism from opponents who portray him as an elite politician more comfortable with Bangkok’s establishment than with the rural voters who repeatedly backed Thaksin-aligned parties.

At the time he became prime minister, Abhisit was in his mid-40s, making him one of the youngest leaders in modern Thai history.

## A fragile coalition

Abhisit’s government rests on a coalition assembled after the court-ordered dissolution of the ruling party. That gives him a path to power, but not necessarily a strong mandate in the eyes of his critics.

Supporters say his leadership offers Thailand a chance to restore stability, repair investor confidence and move beyond street politics. Opponents say his government was born not from a general election, but from political maneuvering after judicial intervention — a charge that could fuel renewed protests by Thaksin supporters, later widely associated with the “Red Shirt” movement.

Managing that legitimacy problem may be Abhisit’s most immediate political challenge.

## Economic pressures mount

Thailand’s political crisis has arrived alongside the global financial downturn of 2008, leaving the new government with limited room for error. Tourism, one of the country’s most important industries, was badly hit by the airport shutdown and by images of chaos broadcast around the world.

Exporters are also under pressure as global demand weakens. Investors are watching closely to see whether the new administration can provide stability after years of coups, protests and shifting governments.

Abhisit is expected to focus on economic stimulus, restoring confidence and reassuring foreign governments and businesses that Thailand remains open and governable.

## Deep divisions remain

Beyond the economy, Abhisit faces long-running national challenges: political polarization, questions about the role of the courts and military in politics, and an insurgency in Thailand’s predominantly Muslim southern provinces.

The conflict between pro- and anti-Thaksin forces is unlikely to disappear quickly. Thaksin, living abroad to avoid a corruption conviction he says was politically motivated, continues to command loyalty among many voters, especially in the north and northeast.

For Abhisit, the test will be whether he can govern beyond his base, calm the streets and convince skeptical voters that his administration represents more than a temporary victory for Thaksin’s opponents.

Thailand has a new prime minister. Whether it has a path out of crisis remains far less certain.

Abhisit, leader of the Democrat Party, became prime minister in December 2008 after a dramatic parliamentary realignment. His ascent followed a Constitutional Court ruling that dissolved the ruling People Power Party, which was aligned with former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, and banned several of its leaders from politics. Supporters of Thaksin accused Abhisit of benefiting from judicial intervention and backroom political deals rather than a general election. The coup was justified by its leaders as a response to corruption allegations and political conflict, but it polarized the country and set the stage for a long struggle between Thaksin’s supporters and opponents.

That struggle intensified in 2008 when the People’s Alliance for Democracy, known as the “Yellow Shirts,” staged prolonged demonstrations against pro-Thaksin governments. The protests culminated in the seizure of Bangkok’s Suvarnabhumi and Don Mueang airports, stranding hundreds of thousands of travelers and severely damaging Thailand’s tourism-dependent economy.

In his CNN interview, Abhisit acknowledged the seriousness of the airport shutdown and the political unrest that preceded his premiership. He said his government would seek reconciliation while restoring the rule of law and preventing future disruptions.

Abhisit’s polished style and elite background have made him a familiar figure internationally. Born in England and educated at Oxford, he has often been viewed as a contrast to Thailand’s more populist political figures. But at home, he faces the difficult task of proving that his government represents more than Bangkok’s establishment and military-aligned interests.

His immediate challenges include reviving an economy hit by the global financial crisis and political instability, addressing anger among Thaksin’s “Red Shirt” supporters, and demonstrating that democratic institutions can function without military intervention or street pressure.

For now, Abhisit is presenting himself as a constitutional leader determined to move Thailand beyond crisis. But the divisions exposed by the 2006 coup, the airport protests and the contested nature of his rise to power remain unresolved — and they are likely to define his premiership.

Thaksin, a billionaire telecoms tycoon, had been elected prime minister in 2001 and won strong support among rural and working-class voters through populist policies. But he was accused by opponents—especially royalist, military, and urban middle-class groups—of corruption, authoritarianism, and undermining Thailand’s monarchy-linked establishment. He was ousted in a **2006 military coup** and later went into exile to avoid a corruption conviction. Even outside the country, he remained the dominant figure in Thai politics through allied parties.

After the coup, pro-Thaksin forces returned to power in the 2007 election under the **People Power Party (PPP)**, widely seen as a successor to Thaksin’s banned Thai Rak Thai party.

- **Samak Sundaravej**, a veteran politician and Thaksin ally, became prime minister in early 2008. His government faced fierce street protests by the anti-Thaksin **People’s Alliance for Democracy (PAD)**, known as the “Yellow Shirts.” In September 2008, Thailand’s Constitutional Court removed Samak from office for violating conflict-of-interest rules by accepting payment for hosting a TV cooking show while prime minister.

- He was replaced by **Somchai Wongsawat**, another PPP figure and Thaksin’s brother-in-law. Somchai’s premiership was also engulfed by protests. PAD demonstrators occupied government buildings and later Bangkok’s airports, demanding an end to what they saw as Thaksin’s proxy rule. In December 2008, the Constitutional Court dissolved the PPP for electoral fraud and banned its executives from politics, forcing Somchai from office.

With the pro-Thaksin governing party disbanded, several factions and smaller parties shifted allegiance. The opposition **Democrat Party**, led by **Abhisit Vejjajiva**, was then able to assemble a parliamentary coalition. Abhisit’s rise was therefore not the result of a general election victory, but of court rulings, party defections, military and establishment pressure, and the collapse of two successive Thaksin-aligned governments.

His appointment made him Thailand’s **third prime minister in four months**, reflecting the deep polarization between pro-Thaksin electoral majorities and anti-Thaksin establishment forces that had dominated Thai politics since the 2006 coup.

## Abhisit Vejjajiva: The Oxford-educated reformer who struggled to heal Thailand’s political divide

**Bangkok, Thailand —** Abhisit Vejjajiva entered Thai politics with the résumé of a modern technocrat: British-born, Eton-educated, Oxford-trained and fluent in the language of liberal democracy. But his time at the center of Thai power was defined less by policy reform than by one of the country’s most turbulent political eras — a period marked by street protests, fragile coalitions, military influence and deadly confrontation.

As Thailand’s prime minister from 2008 to 2011, Abhisit cast himself as a constitutional democrat trying to restore stability after years of political crisis. His critics, however, saw him as the beneficiary of elite maneuvering and an establishment order determined to contain the political movement associated with former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra.

### Elite education, reformist image

Born in Newcastle, England, in 1964 to a prominent Thai family, Abhisit was educated at **Eton College** before studying **Philosophy, Politics and Economics at the University of Oxford**, where he later also earned a master’s degree in economics. His polished English, measured speaking style and international outlook helped distinguish him from many Thai political contemporaries.

After returning to Thailand, he became an academic briefly before entering politics with the **Democrat Party**, Thailand’s oldest political party. He won a parliamentary seat in Bangkok in 1992 and quickly rose through the party’s ranks, gaining a reputation as articulate, clean and policy-focused.

By 2005, Abhisit had become leader of the Democrat Party. But his ascent came during a period in which Thai politics was being transformed by Thaksin, whose populist economic policies drew massive support from rural and working-class voters while alarming urban conservatives, royalists and parts of the military establishment.

### Rise to power through a coalition

Abhisit became prime minister in December 2008 after a court dissolved the pro-Thaksin People Power Party, which had won the previous election. Parliament then selected Abhisit to lead a coalition government made up of the Democrat Party and smaller parties, including factions that had previously supported pro-Thaksin governments.

His supporters argued the process was constitutional and necessary to restore order after months of instability, including the occupation of Bangkok’s airports by anti-Thaksin “Yellow Shirt” protesters.

But opponents said his rise reflected backroom deal-making backed by powerful unelected forces, including the military. For the pro-Thaksin “Red Shirt” movement, Abhisit’s premiership symbolized a system in which election victories by Thaksin-aligned parties could be overturned by courts, protests and elite pressure.

That legitimacy problem would haunt his government.

### Governing amid crisis

Abhisit’s administration faced an immediate challenge: managing an economy hit by the global financial crisis while trying to calm a deeply polarized country. His government introduced stimulus measures, social welfare programs and economic support packages, including policies aimed at low-income Thais.

He sought to present himself as a moderate reformer — committed to parliamentary democracy, rule of law and reconciliation. But the political conflict only intensified.

In 2009 and again in 2010, Red Shirt protesters mobilized in Bangkok, demanding new elections. The movement argued that Abhisit lacked a genuine electoral mandate and that Thailand’s democratic process had been repeatedly distorted to block Thaksin-aligned governments.

The standoff culminated in the **2010 crackdown on Red Shirt protests**, when security forces moved to clear demonstrators from central Bangkok. More than 90 people were killed over weeks of unrest, including protesters, soldiers, medics and journalists. The violence became the defining controversy of Abhisit’s premiership.

### Criticism and accountability questions

Abhisit has long defended his government’s handling of the 2010 crisis, arguing that authorities faced armed elements among protesters and that the state had a duty to restore order. He has said his government sought negotiation before using force.

Critics reject that defense, accusing his administration of authorizing a military operation that used excessive force and failed to adequately protect civilians. Human rights groups raised concerns over live ammunition, emergency powers, detention practices and restrictions on media.

The events deepened mistrust between Thailand’s political camps. For many Red Shirt supporters, the crackdown became a symbol of unequal justice — with protesters facing prosecution while senior officials and military commanders avoided meaningful accountability.

Abhisit’s government also drew criticism over censorship and use of strict security laws, including emergency decrees and computer crime provisions. During his tenure, Thailand saw increased pressure on media outlets linked to the opposition, as well as continued controversy over prosecutions under the country’s strict lèse-majesté laws.

### Efforts to reunite Thailand

Despite the confrontations, Abhisit repeatedly framed reconciliation as a central goal. His government proposed a political “road map” that included constitutional reform discussions, investigations into violence, media reform and eventual elections.

He backed reconciliation committees and compensation efforts for victims of political unrest. He also attempted to bridge Thailand’s rural-urban divide through welfare and economic support programs, seeking to blunt the appeal of Thaksin-style populism without fully embracing it.

But those efforts were overshadowed by questions of legitimacy and the trauma of 2010. Reconciliation proved difficult in a country where rival political camps disagreed not only over policy, but over the rules of the democratic game itself.

In 2011, Abhisit called elections. His Democrat Party lost decisively to **Yingluck Shinawatra**, Thaksin’s sister, whose victory underscored the enduring strength of the political movement Abhisit had struggled to contain. He stepped down as party leader, though he was later re-elected to the post.

### Later role and legacy

Abhisit remained an important voice in Thai politics after leaving office, often positioning himself as a principled conservative democrat. He criticized both Thaksin-style majoritarian politics and military intervention, though critics argued that the Democrat Party had benefited from establishment power structures.

His later career reflected the shrinking space for traditional party politics in Thailand. After the 2014 military coup, Thai politics was reshaped again under military rule. In 2019, Abhisit resigned as a member of parliament after his party moved toward supporting former junta leader Prayuth Chan-ocha as prime minister — a decision that appeared consistent with his stated opposition to extending military-backed rule.

Abhisit’s legacy remains sharply divided. To admirers, he is a thoughtful, internationally minded politician who tried to preserve constitutional politics during a period of chaos. To opponents, he is remembered as a leader who came to power without a direct electoral mandate and presided over one of the deadliest crackdowns in modern Thai history.

His career captures the central contradiction of Thailand’s recent politics: the struggle to reconcile electoral democracy with entrenched institutions, mass movements and competing claims of legitimacy. For Abhisit Vejjajiva, the ambition was to reunite Thailand. The reality was that his years in power revealed just how divided the country had become.

counterfactuals.output:
# Abhisit Vejjajiva and the Significance of His Rise During Thailand’s Constitutional Crisis

Abhisit Vejjajiva is a Thai politician, former leader of the Democrat Party, and Thailand’s prime minister from 2008 to 2011. When he was chosen by parliament to become prime minister in December 2008, he was in his mid-40s, making him Thailand’s youngest prime minister in decades. His selection came at a moment of deep political turmoil, following months of street protests, judicial interventions, and instability that exposed the fragility of Thailand’s democratic institutions.

## Who Is Abhisit Vejjajiva?

Abhisit was born in 1964 in Newcastle upon Tyne, England, to a prominent Thai family. He was educated at Eton College and Oxford University, where he studied philosophy, politics, and economics. His polished international background, fluent English, and technocratic image helped shape his reputation as a modern, articulate conservative politician.

He entered Thai politics in the early 1990s as a member of the Democrat Party, one of Thailand’s oldest political parties. Over time, he became known as a reform-minded figure within the party and eventually rose to become its leader. The Democrat Party’s main base of support was traditionally in Bangkok, southern Thailand, and among middle-class and establishment-oriented voters.

Abhisit’s political identity was often contrasted with that of Thaksin Shinawatra, the billionaire telecommunications tycoon who became prime minister in 2001 and transformed Thai politics through populist policies that appealed strongly to rural and working-class voters. While Thaksin’s movement drew support from the north and northeast, Abhisit’s party represented many voters who were skeptical of Thaksin’s dominance and accused him of corruption, authoritarian tendencies, and conflicts of interest.

## The Crisis That Brought Him to Power

Abhisit became prime minister during a prolonged constitutional and political crisis that followed the 2006 military coup, which had ousted Thaksin Shinawatra. Although Thaksin was removed from office, parties aligned with him continued to win elections, showing the depth of his support among Thai voters.

In 2007, after a new constitution was adopted under military influence, elections brought a pro-Thaksin party, the People’s Power Party, to power. But anti-Thaksin forces remained powerful in the courts, military, bureaucracy, and street protest movements.

In 2008, Thailand was shaken by demonstrations led by the People’s Alliance for Democracy, known as the “Yellow Shirts.” The protesters accused the elected government of being a proxy for Thaksin and demanded political changes that would reduce the influence of electoral majorities. Their campaign culminated in the dramatic occupation of Bangkok’s airports, stranding travelers and paralyzing the country.

The crisis reached a turning point when Thailand’s Constitutional Court dissolved the ruling People’s Power Party and banned several of its leaders from politics over electoral fraud charges. Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat, Thaksin’s brother-in-law, was removed from office. This judicial decision reshaped parliament and opened the way for a new coalition government.

Abhisit did not come to power through a general election. Instead, he was selected by a parliamentary vote after several factions shifted their allegiance away from the pro-Thaksin camp and backed the Democrat Party. His rise was therefore legal under parliamentary rules, but politically controversial.

## Why His Selection Was Significant

Abhisit’s selection was significant for several reasons.

First, his age symbolized a generational change. At 44, he was younger than most Thai leaders before him and projected an image of modern, educated, internationally connected leadership. To supporters, he represented stability, competence, and a chance to restore Thailand’s credibility after months of unrest.

Second, his rise marked a victory for anti-Thaksin forces. The Democrat Party had repeatedly failed to defeat Thaksin-aligned parties in national elections. Abhisit’s path to power through parliamentary realignment, following a court ruling, showed that the struggle for control of Thailand was not being fought only at the ballot box. Courts, protest movements, coalition bargaining, and the military all played decisive roles.

Third, his premiership highlighted Thailand’s constitutional dilemma. The crisis raised difficult questions about democratic legitimacy: If pro-Thaksin parties kept winning elections, could their removal by courts and pressure from street protests be seen as democratic? Conversely, if elected governments abused power or violated election laws, what role should courts and constitutional bodies play? Abhisit’s government sat at the center of these unresolved tensions.

Fourth, his selection deepened Thailand’s political divide. Many urban middle-class voters and royalist conservatives welcomed him as a lawful and stabilizing leader. But many Thaksin supporters, later associated with the “Red Shirt” movement, saw his government as the product of elite maneuvering rather than the popular will. This perception would later fuel mass protests against Abhisit’s administration, especially in 2009 and 2010.

## A Prime Minister in a Divided Country

Abhisit inherited a country split between competing visions of democracy. One side emphasized elections and majority rule, especially the political voice of rural voters who had benefited from Thaksin-era policies. The other side emphasized checks and balances, anti-corruption measures, loyalty to traditional institutions, and fear of what it saw as elected authoritarianism.

His government also faced major practical challenges: restoring confidence after the airport seizures, managing the economy during the global financial crisis, and containing political unrest. Although Abhisit promoted himself as a democratic reformer, his administration was also criticized for relying on support from the military and establishment forces.

The most serious challenge came from the Red Shirt protests, which accused his government of lacking a genuine electoral mandate. In 2010, a military crackdown on Red Shirt demonstrators in Bangkok led to dozens of deaths and became one of the most traumatic episodes in modern Thai politics.

## Conclusion

Abhisit Vejjajiva’s selection as Thailand’s youngest prime minister in decades was more than a personal milestone. It was a defining moment in Thailand’s constitutional crisis. His rise reflected the collapse of one government, the intervention of the courts, the power of street protests, and the shifting alliances of parliament.

To his supporters, Abhisit represented a youthful, capable leader who could restore order after chaos. To his critics, he embodied the ability of Thailand’s establishment to block or reverse the electoral strength of Thaksin-aligned parties. His premiership therefore symbolized the central conflict in Thai politics: the unresolved struggle between electoral democracy, constitutional oversight, elite power, and popular legitimacy.
